newsitem.title: USA: SEC told by lawmakers to rework derivatives rules.
newsitem.headline: SEC told by lawmakers to rework derivatives rules.

text.p: A Senate panel has asked the Securities and Exchange Commisson to go back to the drawing board, re-work and test controversial rules requiring firms to disclose more information about the derivatives they hold.
In a bi-partisan report sent to the agency late yesterday, the Securities Subcommittee of Senate Banking Committee told the SEC to delay using the new rules until they are improved.
"The application of the rules should be extended only after the Commission has carefully considered these results and made any changes," the Senate panel recommended in the report.
The panel has asked the agency to narrow the application of the rules to a smaller sample, use that as a pilot program and draw up conclusions based on those trials, a Senate aide said.

Despite widespread opposition from companies and others, the SEC earlier this year approved its derivatives rules, which it wants to phase in over 1997 and 1998. The rules require companies to disclose the value of their derivatives holdings and any potential risks.
Now the agency is left with little choice but to follow lawmakers' recommendations since the rules face the threat of being overturned altogether.

Texas Senator Phil Gramm, who chairs the subcommittee that issued the report, and Rep. David McIntosh of Indiana, who chairs the regulatory subcommittee of the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee, are considering overturning the agency's rules. They have until early May to introduce a resolution to do so quickly under the Congressional Review Act.

"We need to hear something from the SEC very soon," the chief counsel to McIntosh's subcommittee said, adding that the chairman agrees with the report's findings and is going to press the SEC about making the changes.

SEC officials, including commissioner Steven Wallman, have said the new rules are a plus for investors. They maintain that the rules have been modified enough to address concerns that were raised by the industry.

But still the subcommittee in its April 21 report questioned the value of the SEC rules in addition to the effectiveness of separate derivatives accounting rules being written by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB).
The Senate panel called the SEC and FASB rules unnecessary and burdensome.

Both proposals "perversely create the potential to present to investors a distorted and misledaing picture of company conditions and activities," the panel wrote. "The SEC and FASB rules could reduce the willingness of companies to use derivatives to manage risk."

Further, the subcommittee accused the agency of doing little analysis of the cost the rules would place on firms, which it said is a violation of the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996.
"The SEC rules might not have been drafted in ways that raise such serious concerns about costs to American business and misinformation for American investors," the panel said.
In addition to modifying the rules, the SEC was told to make better use of the agency's economists when designing new regulations, a promise SEC chairman Arthur Levitt has already made to the panel.
FASB, in light of the overwhelming concerns raised by the derivatives industry, was told by the subcommittee to rework its rules rather than issue a final version later this Spring.
The lawmakers' recommendations came as good news to some industry sources.

"The findings and recommendations in the subcommittee report show the increasing awareness in Congress that the SEC and FASB regulations may be harmful to a broad segment of the economy," said Mark Brickell, a director of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association and a managing director at J.P. Morgan.
